what: The dialogue with a materialist king who tests for the soul by experiments on criminals: Keśin and Paesi (Rājapraśnīya) / Kumāra Kassapa and Pāyāsi (DN 23)

evidence.detail: Same king-name (Paesi / Pāyāsi), same experiments, similar similes; direction unknown or a shared older story

what: Shared ascetic stories and verses: Nami's renunciation (Utt 9; Mahājanaka and Nimi jātakas), Harikeśa (Utt 12; Mātaṅga jātaka), Citta and Sambhūta (Utt 13; Cittasambhūta jātaka), Iṣukāra (Utt 14; Hatthipāla jātaka), the true brāhmaṇa (Utt 25; Dhammapada 26)

evidence.detail: Parallel narratives and near-identical verses; usually explained as a common stock of śramaṇa poetry

what: Sayings attributed to seers of other traditions (Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Asita Devala; also the Buddhist Śāriputra and Mahākāśyapa, and Gośāla) received into a Jain collection as the words of 'arhat-ṛṣis'

evidence.detail: The Isibhāsiyāiṃ names the seers and gives each a teaching

what: The Rāma story, retold and corrected: Rāma non-violent and liberated, Lakṣmaṇa the slayer of Rāvaṇa, Rāvaṇa a learned vidyādhara, the 'monkeys' and 'demons' human clans

evidence.detail: The Paumacariya frames its telling as a correction of the popular Rāmāyaṇa, which it calls false

what: Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, the Pāṇḍavas and Dvārakā woven into the life of the Tīrthaṅkara Nemi as his cousins; Kṛṣṇa a vāsudeva who goes to hell and will be a future Tīrthaṅkara
The Jīvandhara (Cīvakaṉ) story, from Guṇabhadra's Uttarapurāṇa and Vādībhasiṃha's works, recast as the Tamil epic Cīvakacintāmaṇi

evidence.detail: Same plot and names; the Tamil epic expands the romance

what: The Jain tradition's claim that the schismatic Rohagupta (Ṣaḍulūka) founded the Vaiśeṣika system with its six categories
era: claimed for the 1st c. CE (Jain chronology)

evidence.detail: Āvaśyaka commentaries and the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya; not accepted by Vaiśeṣika sources, which ascribe their system to Kaṇāda
